client: Lately, I’ve been feeling this deep sadness that I just can’t shake. Ever since my grandmother passed away last month, I keep thinking about her and how much I miss her, and it’s made me start questioning my own future—like, what’s the point of anything if we all just end up gone? I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this, though. It feels like something I just have to live with.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're missing your grandmother and how her passing has stirred these big questions about life's meaning. While your words express sadness, I notice your voice sounds a bit more detached—almost like part of you is trying to hold this grief at arm's length. Would you be willing to share what it's like when you let yourself really feel that sadness?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess I do feel detached sometimes—like I'm watching myself grieve from a distance. When I really let the sadness in, it's overwhelming, and I start thinking about how final death is and how I'll never see her again. It feels easier to stay numb than to face that pain head-on.
therapist: It sounds like you're describing two different experiences—the numbness that feels safer and the overwhelming pain that comes when you fully connect with your loss. I notice your voice becomes more animated when you talk about the pain—would you say there's almost a relief in letting yourself feel it, even though it's intense?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Yeah, I guess there is a kind of relief when I stop fighting the pain. But it scares me too—like if I really let myself feel it, I might drown in it. The numbness feels safer, even if it makes me feel empty and disconnected from everything.
therapist: It sounds like you're walking a careful line between honoring your grief and protecting yourself from being overwhelmed by it. I notice your voice carries more emotion when you describe both the relief and the fear—it seems like this is a very real and important tension for you. What would it be like to explore ways to dip into those feelings in manageable doses, rather than worrying about being completely overwhelmed?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I don't know... the idea of intentionally dipping into those painful feelings scares me. What if I can't stop once I start? Last time I really let myself feel it, I couldn't function for days. 

But part of me does wonder if constantly pushing it away is making things worse. I just don't trust myself to handle it in small doses like you're suggesting. It feels like opening a door I won't be able to close.
therapist: You're describing such an understandable fear—that once you open the door to these feelings, they might flood in uncontrollably. I hear both the wisdom in your caution and the part of you that recognizes how exhausting it is to keep pushing them away. Would it help if we explored some concrete ways to create safety measures—like setting time limits or having grounding techniques ready—before opening that door?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying about safety measures, but honestly the idea of even cracking the door open scares me. What if the time limit passes and I'm still drowning in it? I've had panic attacks before where grounding techniques just... didn't work when I needed them most.
therapist: I hear how frightening that prospect feels—like the pain might override any safety measures you try to put in place. Your voice sounds quieter and more hesitant as you describe this, like part of you is already bracing for that overwhelming experience. Would it feel safer if we started by just noticing when small waves of grief come up naturally, rather than intentionally inviting them in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, maybe noticing the small waves could help... but sometimes even those feel too big. Like if I start letting myself feel even a little bit of it, the whole dam might break. I'm scared I won't be able to stop crying if I start. 

And part of me thinks - what's the point? The grief isn't going anywhere. Why poke at it?
therapist: I hear how much fear comes up around even small waves of grief—like your body is bracing against something that feels unstoppable. Your words and voice both carry that mix of sadness and anxiety, especially when you talk about the dam breaking. Would it help if we explored what "the dam breaking" might actually look like—not as a catastrophic flood, but as your body's natural way of processing this loss?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don’t know, the idea of the dam breaking still feels terrifying to me. I’m scared that if I let myself feel it, I’ll just get overwhelmed and won’t be able to function. It’s like I’ve been holding it together for so long, and I’m afraid of what might happen if I stop.
therapist: I hear how much energy it's taking to hold everything together, and how terrifying it feels to imagine letting go of that control. Your voice sounds both urgent and weary as you describe this—like part of you is exhausted from the effort of keeping the dam intact. Could we explore what "functioning" looks like to you right now, and whether holding everything in might actually be costing you more than you realize?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don’t know, functioning just means not falling apart. If I let go, everything will collapse. But you’re right—it’s exhausting. The idea of loosening control terrifies me because what if I can’t put the pieces back together? It feels like the only thing keeping me safe is keeping everything tightly managed.
therapist: I hear how tightly you're holding onto this idea of control as your lifeline—like it's the only thing preventing total collapse. Your voice sounds quieter and more strained as you say this, almost like the effort of maintaining that control is taking its toll. What would it be like to imagine that "falling apart" might actually look more like *resting* than collapsing—like your system finally getting the chance to release what it's been carrying?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: That idea makes me really uncomfortable. If I let go of control even for a second, I'm scared everything will spiral—my work will fall behind, people will be disappointed in me, I'll become a complete mess. Resting feels like laziness, not recovery.
therapist: I hear how deeply intertwined control and self-worth feel for you—like any slip could unravel not just your emotions, but how others see you. Your voice sounds tense and higher-pitched as you describe this, like you're bracing against an invisible weight. Could we explore where this belief that rest equals laziness comes from? It sounds like it's been carrying a lot of power over how you treat yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know...it's just how I was raised, I guess. My parents were always working, always stressed, and they'd say things like "idle hands are the devil's workshop." Now when I try to relax, I just feel guilty, like I'm wasting time. 

But sometimes I wonder if it's more than that—like maybe if I stop being productive, people will realize I'm not actually that impressive or capable. That thought terrifies me.
therapist: It sounds like these messages about productivity and worth run very deep—both from your upbringing and from your fears about being "found out." I notice your voice speeds up when you talk about that fear, like part of you is racing to outrun it. What do you imagine might happen if someone *did* see you in a moment of rest—what's the worst-case scenario your mind is trying to prevent?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
